stories.title: India sends first tranche of relief supplies to earthquake-hit Colombia
stories.summary: External Affairs Minister (EAM) S Jaishankar expressed India's solidarity with the people of Colombia during these difficult times.

opening: External Affairs Minister (EAM) S Jaishankar expressed India's solidarity with the people of Colombia during these difficult times.

New Delhi, August 14: India on Friday dispatched the first tranche of 20 metric tonnes of relief supplies to Colombia to support recovery efforts following a devastating earthquake that struck the country earlier this week.
body: External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar said the assistance includes medicines and medical equipment, temporary shelters, hygiene supplies and other essential items required in the aftermath of the disaster.

“Dispatched the first tranche of the 20 MT relief supplies to Colombia to support ongoing post-earthquake recovery efforts,” Jaishankar said in a post on X, expressing India's solidarity with the people of Colombia during the difficult period.
The assistance highlights India's role as a first responder in humanitarian emergencies and natural disasters.
The magnitude 7.3 earthquake struck western Colombia on Monday, killing 281 people and injuring 3,971, while 391 people remain missing.
According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake struck at 7:34 a.m. local time, with its epicentre near San Jose del Palmar at a depth of 96 kilometres.
The National Unit for Disaster Risk Management said 44,936 families, comprising more than 102,000 people, across 15 departments and 426 municipalities have been affected.
Around 10,677 homes were destroyed, while another 65,841 sustained damage.
On Tuesday, Jaishankar had expressed condolences to the families of those killed and prayed for the speedy recovery of those injured.
He had also said that India was ready to extend all possible assistance to Colombia.
The latest relief shipment reinforces India's commitment to providing timely humanitarian assistance and standing in solidarity with countries affected by major natural disasters.

stories.headline: India's generosity, tolerance should not be mistaken for weakness: NSA Ajit Doval on Operation Sindoor
stories.title: India's generosity, tolerance should not be mistaken for weakness: NSA Ajit Doval on Operation Sindoor
stories.summary: New Delhi, Aug 14: National Security Advisor Ajit Doval has said India's generosity and tolerance should not be mistaken for weakness, asserting that the country can take risks and hit hard, irrespective of the consequences. Speaking in the upcoming Discovery docuseries "Declassified: Operation Sindoor", Doval said the objective of the 88-hour military operation was to destroy enemy camps, particularly those responsible for the Pahalgam terror attack. "We had decided the objective of the operation as destruction of the enemy camps particularly those who had been responsible for the Pahalgam attack," Doval said in his first interview since Operation Sindoor. "Message to the world is very clear - India’s generosity or India being tolerant should not be mistaken for its weakness. India can take risks, India can hit hard, irrespective of the consequences," he added. The two-part docuseries brings together India's military and national security leadership to recount the decisions and events surrounding Operation Sindoor, with first-hand accounts from those who oversaw India’s response, Discovery said in a statement. In the show, Doval offers an account of the decision-making and resolve behind the military response, it added. "Declassified: Operation Sindoor" will premiere on Saturday at 9 pm on Discovery and streaming service discovery+. Operation Sindoor was launched early on May 7 last year to avenge the deadly April 22 Pahalgam terror attack, with Indian forces conducting precision strikes on multiple terror infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK). Pakistan later also launched offensives against India, and all subsequent counter-offensives by India were also carried out under Operation Sindoor. The military conflict between the two nuclear-armed neighbours, lasting nearly 88 hours, halted after they reached an understanding on the evening of May 10.

stories.headline: LG Sinha Addresses Partition Horrors Remembrance Day event at Srinagar
stories.title: LG Sinha Addresses Partition Horrors Remembrance Day event at Srinagar
stories.summary: SRINAGAR, AUGUST 14: The Lieutenant Governor, Manoj Sinha today attended the solemn observance of ‘Partition Horrors Remembrance Day’ at Tagore Hall, Srinagar. The event was marked by collective remembrance and a reaffirmation of national unity. In his address on the occasion, the Lieutenant Governor paid heartfelt tribute to all those citizens who endured unimaginable suffering during the partition of 1947 and whose sacrifices continue to inspire generations. The Lieutenant Governor emphasized that the wound of partition continues to exist as a pain in the collective consciousness of every Indian. “Decades after the partition, their sacrifice reminds us that the wound remains unhealed, lingering as a generational pain in India's collective soul. On Partition Horrors Remembrance Day, we are not merely recalling the past but we are giving voice to those millions whose voices were taken away from them. I wish to reiterate with firm resolve that we will not allow their pain to be buried in the dust of history. Remembering them is fulfilling our duty towards humanity. We will preserve their memories. Remembering them with complete truthfulness, honesty, and utmost sensitivity is the most sacred tribute. I believe that their stories are an indelible chapter of our national consciousness, and their sacrifice will forever remain alive in the soul of Mother India,” the Lieutenant Governor said. The Lieutenant Governor urged the people of UT of Jammu Kashmir to treat this day as an occasion of introspection and national resolve. He called upon the youth, farmers, workers, and women to rise with courage and determination, to turn the pace of time towards progress and harmony. The Lieutenant Governor praised the resilience of people who rebuilt their lives with courage and enriched the country’s social fabric and cultural heritage with historic traditions and values. ‘Today’s occasion is an opportunity to acknowledge the pain of the past and strengthen our unwavering commitment to peace, harmony and national unity. This day reminds us that only the lessons of history can make the future secure and humane,” the Lieutenant Governor said. He noted that the partition divided families and displaced communities from Pakistan-occupied Jammu Kashmir and Chhamb. He paid tribute to those who faced decades-long discrimination within the UT due to Article 370. The Lieutenant Governor said that Hon'ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi ended their suffering and granted them equal rights like any other citizen of the country. The Lieutenant Governor also paid tribute the countless families who sacrificed during the tribal invasion months after partition. “Within a few months of partition, enemies of the nation carried out terror attack under the cover of tribal invasions. Indian army and people fought bravely. The struggle and sacrifice of countless families are an integral part of the collective memory of Jammu Kashmir. Today, I humbly pay tribute to the patience, hard work, and unbroken patriotism of all those families,” he said. Addressing the youth, the Lieutenant Governor emphasized that partition is not merely history but a living memory of millions of families. He urged them to learn from the experiences of the past, to reject enmity and communal bitterness, and to build bridges of trust. He called upon them to construct a developed India that is inclusive and empowered. "The youth of Jammu Kashmir must ensure that the mistakes of the past are never repeated in the future. Where walls were once raised, you must build bridges of trust and construct a Viksit Bharat that is inclusive,” the Lieutenant Governor said. The Lieutenant Governor reminded the gathering that India’s strength lies in its diversity. From Kashmir to Kanyakumari, from Gujarat to Goa, from Assam to Arunachal Pradesh, India is a confluence of languages, cultures, traditions, and beliefs, he said. “Through partition, enemies of the nation tried to destroy this spirit of unity in diversity, but India has continuously moved forward with pride and confidence. We must take a pledge to acquaint future generations with the pain of partition, to strengthen peace and harmony, and to ensure that such a tragedy is never repeated. Building a self-reliant Jammu Kashmir is a shared duty and national unity remains the bedrock of our strength, security and collective progress,” the Lieutenant Governor said. The Lieutenant Governor visited the photo exhibition on Partition Horrors Remembrance Day. A Two- minute silence was observed in the memory of those who lost their lives during the Partition of India. The event also featured a moving theatrical performance by the artists that brought to light the trauma, hardship, and displacement experienced by millions during the Partition. Dr Syed Darakhshan Andrabi, Chairperson, J&K Waqf Board; Shri Atal Dulloo, Chief Secretary; Shri Shaleen Kabra, Additional Chief Secretary, Jal Shakti Department, Shri Brij Mohan Sharma, Principal Secretary Culture; Shri Ashok Koul, General Secretary (Organisation) BJP J&K; senior officials, prominent citizens from different walks of life and youth in large number were present.

stories.headline: Music for nothing and clicks for free: The bane of streaming platforms in India
stories.title: Music for nothing and clicks for free: The bane of streaming platforms in India
stories.summary: Eighteen-year-old Archit Menon, a college student in Kochi, logs in to two apps the most every day. The first is Instagram, where he scrolls through Reels between classes, half-watching, half-listening; the second is Spotify, where eventually he might find the full version of a song he caught a whiff of on Reels and liked. Most songs on his playlist have been added in this manner.For years he paid nothing for either feed, putting up with the intermittent ads on Spotify, until his consumption increased drastically. “At first I was fine with ads once every 30 minutes. But as I got hooked to my favourite artistes and podcasts, ads started bothering me,” he says. What finally pushed him to pay up was not a discount or a marketing nudge, but the fact that he now wanted to access his playlists while offline, better sound quality that did justice to his Bose headphones, and not letting his music queue be interrupted. “I’m not paying for the songs only but also the seamlessness,” he says.When services like Saavn (later JioSaavn) and Gaana launched in India in 2007 and 2010 respectively, the country’s smartphone and internet industries were nascent, and music platforms were primarily internet-based. Global music streaming platforms entered the Indian market in 2018-2019, with the launch of Amazon Music and Spotify AB. Yatish Mehrishi, CEO, ENIL, under which Gaana operates. photo by Swapnil Sakhare for Forbes IndiaWhen the global players launched their services in countries like the US and Europe, they had paid subscriptions as their core offering, with free listening used to nudge users to upgrade. But when these platforms came to India, they focussed on building a large listenership, and did this through free music. The battle was about getting the largest slice of India’s massive population pie. But now that the same population has gotten hooked to free content and occasional ads—much like All India Radio and FM radio that preceded streaming—getting this listenership to pay is turning out to be a price war.What is queering the pitch further is the fact that listeners are discovering and engaging with music in a fragmented manner across social media platforms such as Instagram, YouTube Shorts, concerts and creator platforms. Thus, no single platform can control the listener’s full journey anymore.The paywall playbook“People often get misled by India’s population of 1.5 billion,” says Yatish Mehrishi, CEO of Entertainment Network India Limited (ENIL) under which Gaana operates. “The assumption was that if you built a habit, everyone would eventually pay. But India is extremely diverse, with significant income disparity. It’s unrealistic to expect the entire population to become paying subscribers.” For years, he says, platforms chased downloads and habit formation, while content costs kept climbing as record labels demanded higher licensing fees, costs that advertising alone could not offset.However, that is starting to change, gradually. According to the FICCI-EY Media & Entertainment Report 2026, India’s paid music subscriptions grew 37 percent in a single year to reach 14.4 million, crossing ₹1,000 crore in audio subscription revenue for the first time. “Paid subscriptions [across platforms] have grown from roughly 7 million to around 15 million over a short period. While those numbers are still modest compared to global markets, they show that consumers are beginning to see value in paying for music,” says Mehrishi. “Indians have paid for music, whether it was LPs, cassettes, CDs or even pirated cassettes. The issue isn’t the ability to pay; it’s the willingness to pay.”Ashish Pherwani, partner for media and entertainment at EY, agrees. “India’s music industry has been providing music for free, or ad-supported, since it got digitised. Indians lost the habit of paying for music over time,” he says. “Global and Indian platforms have now started correcting this anomaly by restricting features to free users, which has helped the paid subscription base to reach about 15 million. We expect that to double in the next three years.” Streaming features such as rewind, offline downloads, unlimited skips and on-demand song selection, once freely available, now need to be paid for. Media reports indicate that platforms, music labels and independent consultants expect the number of paid subscribers to rise to 50-75 million in the next decade.When Amazon Music entered the Indian market, it was with an Amazon Prime-bundled, ad-supported version. “We did not see significant demand for paid premium audio. At the time, the market was dominated by free and telco-bundled offerings, with little differentiation between paid and free services,” says Rishi Mirchandani, vice president of licensing and strategy at Amazon Music.The company launched Amazon Music Unlimited this June, at ₹99 a month for Prime members and ₹119 for others, alongside a new ad-supported Amazon Music Free tier. “Now we’re seeing a shift in India too,” Mirchandani says. “Customers are showing a greater willingness to pay for premium audio experiences.”Rishabh Gupta, head of Amazon Music India, says, “India’s addressable audience for pure-play audio streaming is still expanding. We have a large and growing middle class, and a huge segment of listeners haven’t moved onto pure-play audio streaming. So, for us, acquisition isn’t a phase that’s behind us; it’s ongoing.”Also Read: How India's music makers are charting their own successHowever, he believes, acquisition alone is no longer enough. “Alongside, there’s an equal opportunity to deepen engagement through experiences that reflect how people actually listen,” he says. Amazon Music’s three-tier structure—Prime, Unlimited and Free—is the platform’s attempt to serve every kind of listener. “That’s the real shift for us, from serving one audience to serving all of them.”Amazon’s tiered approach is not unique and is now the industry’s default model. Mehrishi of Gaana predicts India’s audio market will eventually resemble the segmentation seen in video streaming. “Like Netflix or Amazon Prime Video, the market will evolve into multiple segments. Some consumers will subscribe, while others will remain on hybrid or ad-supported models,” he says. Music streaming, he adds, hasn’t seen the rapid subscription growth video experienced during the Covid-19 pandemic, so segmentation will matter more as paid adoption climbs toward 25-30 million users.As of December 2025, India had about 14 million paid music subscriptions, compared to more than 200 million paid video subscriptions, according to a 2026 report by EY and the Indian Music Industry (IMI), titled ‘How India Listens, Streams and Pays for Music’.One of the significant differences between the audio and video streaming industries is that while video streaming platforms have unique content libraries, films or series, the availability of which they shuffle, audio streaming platforms all have the same content libraries, which are available all the time. There is almost nothing that differentiates one platform from another where content is concerned, and their individual unique selling points (USPs) lie in features such as seamless shareability on social media platforms, which can help users discover new music. The unique content of video platforms means a single user may want to subscribe to multiple platforms, while that incentive is not there for users of audio platforms.Andrew Smith, head of digital strategy at Virtuoso Music, which launched in India this June, cites paid listening growth of “more than a third last year” as evidence India is “crossing the line that other markets crossed before it. Every market that closed its free-to-paid gap saw growth take off on the other side,” he says. “It would be no great stretch to suggest India could reach over 140 million paid subscriptions within a decade.”The UK-headquartered company’s India entry marked its first move into South Asia, with a multilingual slate across Hindi, Punjabi, Tamil and Telugu. Virtuoso Music’s head of new business and music, Sahaj Miya, adds, “Paid subscriptions are at the start of their steepest climb, and the next decade of growth for the platforms will be exponential, bringing India much closer to the global operating model.”Not everyone believes progress will be smooth. Pherwani of EY says, “In the long run, the business model that will work will be driven by fans who pay for subscriptions, merchandise and concerts. Advertising and ad-funded content remain adjunct to the main revenue sources for streamers.” This is a reminder that subscriptions, however fast they grow, may never be the whole story. Rishabh Gupta, head, Amazon Music India. Photo by Swapnil Sakhare for Forbes IndiaVolume vs valueThe uncomfortable reality at the centre of India’s streaming story, according to many, is that the country is huge by volume and unremarkable by value. “India records around 5 billion audio and video streams a year, making it one of the largest markets globally by volume. But by value, we are still around the 15th to 20th largest market,” Mehrishi says.That gap, he adds, is not a mystery. The size of India’s population, the large number of films being produced, and linguistic diversity makes monetisation difficult. “Ten years ago, India and China were comparable music markets. Today, China is among the world’s largest by value, while India still ranks around 15th.” According to IFPI’s Global Music Report 2026, globally, recorded music revenue from streaming platforms reached $29.6 billion in 2025, with paid subscriptions rising by 85 million to 837 million. However, India’s contributions in value terms are modest and it ranks 15 in the world where paying listeners are concerned.What India does have, unusually, is an overwhelming preference for its own music, which takes time to find its way onto the platforms, if at all. Domestic collection accounts for roughly 89 percent—among the highest in the world—of all music streaming in the country, according to IFPI data, which is one of the highest home-market shares anywhere in the world. This is one of the reasons global streaming platforms have had to invest heavily in regional catalogues and local artiste partnerships rather than relying solely on international hits. Countries like Japan, South Korea, China and Brazil also prefer their own music compared to international genres.Rajesh Sethi, partner and sector leader for media, entertainment and sports at PwC India, says, “India’s music streaming industry is thriving, powered by smartphone penetration, cheap data, and rising demand for regional content. However, monetisation lags due to price sensitivity and preference for free, ad-supported services. The good news, however, is that consumers are increasingly willing to pay, digital payments are improving, and advertisers are investing in audio too.”In India, the popularity of regional and domestic film and non-film music is an added parameter for platforms to navigate. The share of film music among Indian listeners fell from 65 percent in 2023 to 57 percent in 2025, according to the FICCI-EY report, as independent and regional music took centrestage.Spotify India has watched this play out. “When Spotify launched in India seven years ago, over 70 percent of consumption was international music. Today, that has inverted, with over 70 percent of our consumption being of local content,” says Dhruvank Vaidya, head of music and podcasts. The platform’s artiste-first bets—programmes like RADAR, Rap 91 and I-Pop—were built on the belief that Indian listeners wanted to go beyond film soundtracks if given the option. About half of Spotify India’s annual Top 50 songs are non-film. For instance, Haryanvi music streams have grown nearly sevenfold between 2023 and 2026, spreading well beyond the NCR into cities like Jaipur, Bhopal, Lucknow and Bengaluru.Gupta sees a similar pattern among Amazon Music’s listeners. “The majority of consumption still comes from soundtracks of films or any other videos in India. And the single largest language is still Hindi,” he says; about 83 percent of listeners seek out Hindi music, followed by English and Punjabi, with Tamil and Telugu growing fast; regional breakouts witness spikes in listenership rather than form trends. “We’ll see one-offs: For example, in the last few months, Marathi has been doing really well because of ‘Shaky’ and ‘Gulabi Sadi’. You need a more sustained supply of content in every language and genre. We see those trends across the board, but they’re still sporadic,” says Gupta.Publishing revenue, too, is finding its wings, with creator royalty collections growing more than 40 percent in 2024, among the fastest rates globally, and digital platforms contributing over 80 percent of collections, according to the CISAC Global Collections Report 2025. But ownership and artiste rights remain an issue. Taking advantage of this, Virtuoso’s Miya says the firm is betting on Indian catalogue and artiste ownership because no other platform is focussing on artiste benefits. “The next chapter of the global music story will be written in India,” he says. “We are here to invest in it, bringing our creator-first model built on artist equity.” Unlike the traditional buyout model, with Virtuoso’s revenue model, artistes keep a stake in their music and continue to earn as it generates revenue from streaming and other commercial uses worldwide.Smith adds that India is part of a broader emerging-market pattern: “We have seen it play out globally, with Brazil and Latin America making that shift and compounding ever since. India is crossing that line now, at far greater scale.”Beyond playlistsBesides monetisation, the fragmentation of music consumption is the terrain these platforms have to fight on.A decade ago, Mehrishi says, “Music discovery happened largely through radio. Then YouTube became the primary discovery platform. Today, discovery increasingly happens through Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts.” He is not alarmed by this. “I see this as beneficial for streaming services because music is integral to short-form video. Without music, a Reel is flat. People discover songs through these platforms, and if they like a track, they eventually come to a streaming service to hear the full version.”Sethi adds that these visual, bite-sized formats “speed up discovery-to-listening cycles and boost viral sharing and repeat plays.”Some see the response to fragmentation as not a rewritten business model but as a redefined role. “It’s less about rethinking the business model and more about rethinking what role we want to serve in a listener’s everyday life,” Gupta says. Amazon Music’s answer has been to add exclusive content and experiences in addition to catalogue access. “Because fans want to feel close to the artiste, not just stream them,” Gupta says, pointing to partnering with music releases of films Param Sundari (2025) and Dhurandhar (2026). Devices, too, are part of the strategy: There is a ₹59-a-month Amazon Music Unlimited plan built for Alexa-enabled devices.In the coming years, as Pherwani says, live music and fandom indicate where the industry’s energy and revenue are heading. Mehrishi points to merchandising as an early-stage but inevitable growth line. “Younger audiences have a much stronger sense of fandom than previous generations. They’re willing to spend money on concerts, merchandise and experiences around their favourite artistes.”Vaidya calls it a structural convergence. “Live touring, brand partnerships, sync opportunities—things that were once almost exclusively tied to film music—are now opening up for independent artistes. The boundary between film and non-film has already started to dissolve.”For a market this large and this young, the listening will keep growing; the challenge is to make them pay.

But when these platforms came to India, they focussed on building a large listenership, and did this through free music.
The battle was about getting the largest slice of India’s massive population pie.
But now that the same population has gotten hooked to free content and occasional ads—much like.
All India Radio and FM radio that preceded streaming—getting this listenership to pay is turning out to be a price war.

What is queering the pitch further is the fact that listeners are discovering and engaging with music in a fragmented manner across social media platforms such as Instagram, YouTube Shorts, concerts and creator platforms.
Thus, no single platform can control the listener’s full journey anymore.
The paywall playbook“People often get misled by India’s population of 1.5 billion,” says Yatish Mehrishi, CEO of Entertainment Network India Limited (ENIL) under which Gaana operates.
“The assumption was that if you built a habit, everyone would eventually pay.
But India is extremely diverse, with significant income disparity.

It’s unrealistic to expect the entire population to become paying subscribers.” For years, he says, platforms chased downloads and habit formation, while content costs kept climbing as record labels demanded higher licensing fees, costs that advertising alone could not offset.
However, that is starting to change, gradually.

According to the FICCI-EY Media & Entertainment Report 2026, India’s paid music subscriptions grew 37 percent in a single year to reach 14.4 million, crossing ₹1,000 crore in audio subscription revenue for the first time.
While those numbers are still modest compared to global markets, they show that consumers are beginning to see value in paying for music,” says Mehrishi.
“Indians have paid for music, whether it was LPs, cassettes, CDs or even pirated cassettes.
The issue isn’t the ability to pay; it’s the willingness to pay.” Ashish Pherwani, partner for media and entertainment at EY, agrees.
“India’s music industry has been providing music for free, or ad-supported, since it got digitised.
Indians lost the habit of paying for music over time,” he says.
We expect that to double in the next three years.” Streaming features such as rewind, offline downloads, unlimited skips and on-demand song selection, once freely available, now need to be paid for.
When Amazon Music entered the Indian market, it was with an Amazon Prime-bundled, ad-supported version.
“We did not see significant demand for paid premium audio.

At the time, the market was dominated by free and telco-bundled offerings, with little differentiation between paid and free services,” says Rishi Mirchandani, vice president of licensing and strategy at Amazon Music.
The company launched Amazon Music Unlimited this June, at ₹99 a month for Prime members and ₹119 for others, alongside a new ad-supported Amazon Music Free tier.
“Now we’re seeing a shift in India too,” Mirchandani says.

“Customers are showing a greater willingness to pay for premium audio experiences.” Rishabh Gupta, head of Amazon Music India, says, “India’s addressable audience for pure-play audio streaming is still expanding.
We have a large and growing middle class, and a huge segment of listeners haven’t moved onto pure-play audio streaming.
So, for us, acquisition isn’t a phase that’s behind us; it’s ongoing.” However, he believes, acquisition alone is no longer enough.
“Alongside, there’s an equal opportunity to deepen engagement through experiences that reflect how people actually listen,” he says.
Amazon Music’s three-tier structure—Prime, Unlimited and Free—is the platform’s attempt to serve every kind of listener.
“That’s the real shift for us, from serving one audience to serving all of them.” Amazon’s tiered approach is not unique and is now the industry’s default model.
Mehrishi of Gaana predicts India’s audio market will eventually resemble the segmentation seen in video streaming.
“Like Netflix or Amazon Prime Video, the market will evolve into multiple segments.
Some consumers will subscribe, while others will remain on hybrid or ad-supported models,” he says.

One of the significant differences between the audio and video streaming industries is that while video streaming platforms have unique content libraries, films or series, the availability of which they shuffle, audio streaming platforms all have the same content libraries, which are available all the time.

There is almost nothing that differentiates one platform from another where content is concerned, and their individual unique selling points (USPs) lie in features such as seamless shareability on social media platforms, which can help users discover new music.
The unique content of video platforms means a single user may want to subscribe to multiple platforms, while that incentive is not there for users of audio platforms.

Andrew Smith, head of digital strategy at Virtuoso Music, which launched in India this June, cites paid listening growth of “more than a third last year” as evidence India is “crossing the line that other markets crossed before it.
Every market that closed its free-to-paid gap saw growth take off on the other side,” he says.

Virtuoso Music’s head of new business and music, Sahaj Miya, adds, “Paid subscriptions are at the start of their steepest climb, and the next decade of growth for the platforms will be exponential, bringing India much closer to the global operating model.” Not everyone believes progress will be smooth.
Pherwani of EY says, “In the long run, the business model that will work will be driven by fans who pay for subscriptions, merchandise and concerts.
Advertising and ad-funded content remain adjunct to the main revenue sources for streamers.” This is a reminder that subscriptions, however fast they grow, may never be the whole story.
Rishabh Gupta, head, Amazon Music India.
Photo by Swapnil Sakhare for Forbes IndiaVolume vs value.
The uncomfortable reality at the centre of India’s streaming story, according to many, is that the country is huge by volume and unremarkable by value.
But by value, we are still around the 15th to 20th largest market,” Mehrishi says.
That gap, he adds, is not a mystery.
The size of India’s population, the large number of films being produced, and linguistic diversity makes monetisation difficult.
“Ten years ago, India and China were comparable music markets.
However, India’s contributions in value terms are modest and it ranks 15 in the world where paying listeners are concerned.
What India does have, unusually, is an overwhelming preference for its own music, which takes time to find its way onto the platforms, if at all.
This is one of the reasons global streaming platforms have had to invest heavily in regional catalogues and local artiste partnerships rather than relying solely on international hits.
Countries like Japan, South Korea, China and Brazil also prefer their own music compared to international genres.

Rajesh Sethi, partner and sector leader for media, entertainment and sports at PwC India, says, “India’s music streaming industry is thriving, powered by smartphone penetration, cheap data, and rising demand for regional content.
However, monetisation lags due to price sensitivity and preference for free, ad-supported services.

The good news, however, is that consumers are increasingly willing to pay, digital payments are improving, and advertisers are investing in audio too.” In India, the popularity of regional and domestic film and non-film music is an added parameter for platforms to navigate.
Spotify India has watched this play out.
The platform’s artiste-first bets—programmes like RADAR, Rap 91 and I-Pop—were built on the belief that Indian listeners wanted to go beyond film soundtracks if given the option.
About half of Spotify India’s annual Top 50 songs are non-film.
For instance, Haryanvi music streams have grown nearly sevenfold between 2023 and 2026, spreading well beyond the NCR into cities like Jaipur, Bhopal, Lucknow and Bengaluru.
Gupta sees a similar pattern among Amazon Music’s listeners.
“The majority of consumption still comes from soundtracks of films or any other videos in India.
“We’ll see one-offs: For example, in the last few months, Marathi has been doing really well because of ‘Shaky’ and ‘Gulabi Sadi’.
You need a more sustained supply of content in every language and genre.
We see those trends across the board, but they’re still sporadic,” says Gupta.
But ownership and artiste rights remain an issue.
Taking advantage of this, Virtuoso’s Miya says the firm is betting on Indian catalogue and artiste ownership because no other platform is focussing on artiste benefits.
“The next chapter of the global music story will be written in India,” he says.

“We are here to invest in it, bringing our creator-first model built on artist equity.” Unlike the traditional buyout model, with Virtuoso’s revenue model, artistes keep a stake in their music and continue to earn as it generates revenue from streaming and other commercial uses worldwide.
Smith adds that India is part of a broader emerging-market pattern: “We have seen it play out globally, with Brazil and Latin America making that shift and compounding ever since.
India is crossing that line now, at far greater scale.” Beyond playlistsBesides monetisation, the fragmentation of music consumption is the terrain these platforms have to fight on.
A decade ago, Mehrishi says, “Music discovery happened largely through radio.
Then YouTube became the primary discovery platform.
Today, discovery increasingly happens through Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts.” He is not alarmed by this.
“I see this as beneficial for streaming services because music is integral to short-form video.
Without music, a Reel is flat.

People discover songs through these platforms, and if they like a track, they eventually come to a streaming service to hear the full version.” Sethi adds that these visual, bite-sized formats “speed up discovery-to-listening cycles and boost viral sharing and repeat plays.” Some see the response to fragmentation as not a rewritten business model but as a redefined role.
“It’s less about rethinking the business model and more about rethinking what role we want to serve in a listener’s everyday life,” Gupta says.
Amazon Music’s answer has been to add exclusive content and experiences in addition to catalogue access.
“Because fans want to feel close to the artiste, not just stream them,” Gupta says, pointing to partnering with music releases of films Param Sundari (2025) and Dhurandhar (2026).
Devices, too, are part of the strategy: There is a ₹59-a-month Amazon Music Unlimited plan built for Alexa-enabled devices.
In the coming years, as Pherwani says, live music and fandom indicate where the industry’s energy and revenue are heading.
Mehrishi points to merchandising as an early-stage but inevitable growth line.
“Younger audiences have a much stronger sense of fandom than previous generations.
They’re willing to spend money on concerts, merchandise and experiences around their favourite artistes.” Vaidya calls it a structural convergence.
“Live touring, brand partnerships, sync opportunities—things that were once almost exclusively tied to film music—are now opening up for independent artistes.
The boundary between film and non-film has already started to dissolve.” For a market this large and this young, the listening will keep growing; the challenge is to make them pay.

stories.headline: Military modernisation driven by self-reliant and future-ready defence sector is govt’s top priority: Rajnath Singh
stories.title: Military modernisation driven by self-reliant and future-ready defence sector is govt’s top priority: Rajnath Singh
stories.summary: New Delhi, Aug 14: “The Government, under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, is according the highest priority to the modernisation of the defence forces driven by a self-reliant and future-ready defence sector,” said Defence Minister Rajnath Singh in his address to the soldiers through Akashvani on the eve of 80th Independence Day on August 14, 2026. Highlighting the transformative shift witnessed by the defence sector in the last 12 years due to the initiatives such as ‘Aatmanirbhar Bharat’ and ‘Make-in-India’, Raksha Mantri asserted that India has become a nation which is effectively catering to its own security needs, while emerging as a global defence manufacturing hub and a net defence exporter. Singh emphasised that the domestic defence production, which stood at just Rs 46,000 crore in 2014, has skyrocketed to a record Rs 1.78 lakh crore in the Financial Year (FY) 2025-26, nearly a four-fold increase over the last decade. This achievement, he said, is a testament to the structural changes that have taken place in the defence sector. He pointed out that Defence Public Sector Undertakings (DPSUs) and other public sector entities accounted for approximately 76% of the total defence production, with the private sector contributing 24%, up from 22% in the previous fiscal year. This growing participation of the private sector signals a continuously improving business environment within the defence sector, he said. Defence Minister added that defence exports, which stood at a mere Rs 686 crore in FY 2013-14, surged to an all-time high of Rs 38,424 crore in FY 2025-26, an increase of over 5,500%. He described the feat as the most compelling evidence of Aatmanirbharta in the defence sector. “Today, India has 145 defence exporters, and our products are being exported to over 80 countries. I am confident that we will achieve our defence exports target of Rs 50,000 crore by 2029,” he said. He also pointed out that the defence budget has risen from Rs 2.53 lakh crore in FY 2013-14 to Rs 7.85 lakh crore in FY 2026-27, which is a reflection of India's growing commitment to future defence technologies. “Capital expenditure has grown from Rs 94,588 crore to Rs 2.19 lakh crore. Our focus on Research & Development has also intensified. The R&D budget, which stood at Rs 15,283 crore in FY 2014-15, has increased by 90% to Rs 29,100 crore in FY 2026-27,” he said. Defence Minister added that over the past year, the Defence Acquisition Council has granted Acceptance of Necessity for projects worth over Rs 8.75 lakh crore, which highlights the Government’s emphasis on defence modernisation. He listed the fundamental reforms undertaken in defence procurement to accelerate this modernisation process, including a two-fold increase in financial ceiling for Field Commanders to strengthen operational efficiency, and facilitation of procurement worth more than Rs 1.25 lakh crore through the revenue route to boost indigenisation. Singh acknowledged the enthusiastic participation of the defence forces in the journey towards Aatmanirbharta. He stressed that India’s defence self-reliance drive is gaining momentum as indigenous warships, aircraft and advanced military systems are strengthening the capabilities of the Defence Forces. He asserted that DRDO and the defence forces are positioning India at the forefront of technologies for future warfare amidst the evolving defence landscape. He made special mention of the successful test of the first Tactical Advanced Range Augmentation system, which has the capability to transform conventional weapons into precision-guided munitions. “The testing of the Advanced Agni Missile, equipped with MIRV technology, has added a new dimension to the strategic deterrence capabilities. Successful trials of the Long-Range Land Attack Cruise Missile, RudraM-II Air-to-Surface Missile, Naval Anti-Ship Missile-SR, and Pinaka Long-Range Guided Rocket have provided unprecedented strength to the nation’s strike capabilities,” he added. On the successful test of Active Cooled Full-Scale Scramjet Combustor for over 1,200 seconds, Rajnath Singh stated that the feat has placed India among the select group of nations capable of developing hypersonic missile technology. He added that the nation’s air defence capabilities have been further bolstered by the first successful test of the indigenous Kusha’ Long-Range Surface-to-Air Missile. Defence Minister underlined that border area development is a focus area of the Government as the objective is to enhance defence preparedness and connectivity with border areas. He lauded the defence forces for being the ‘first responders’ to carry out relief and rescue operations whenever an unfortunate natural disaster occurs in the country or abroad. Singh reiterated the Government’s commitment towards the welfare of serving and retired defence forces personnel as well as their families, describing them as a reflection of honor, dignity, and self-respect. “Over the past five years, there has been a 300% increase in the budget of the Ex-Servicemen Contributory Health Scheme. Furthermore, under the Armed Forces Flag Day Fund, the Penury Grant has been doubled from Rs 4,000 to Rs 8,000, the Education Grant from Rs 1,000 to Rs 2,000 and the Marriage Grant from Rs 50,000 to Rs 1,00,000. These decisions demonstrate our commitment to the welfare of our soldiers and their Next-of-Kin,” he said. Raksha Mantri also underscored the Government’s continued focus on providing increased opportunities for women in the defence forces and effectively utilising Nari Shakti in national security & nation building. “We achieved a historic milestone when the first batch of female cadets trained at the National Defence Academy was commissioned as officers in the three Services. This is proof that courage and leadership are not confined to any gender. ‘Samudra Pradakshina’, the first tri-service all-women circumnavigation sailing expedition onboard Indian Army Sailing Vessel Triveni, stands as a symbol of ‘New India’ powered by ‘Nari Shakti’, he said. Singh emphasised that 79 years ago, India’s freedom fighters such as Mahatma Gandhi, Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose, Bhagat Singh, Chandrashekhar Azad, Sarojini Naidu, Rani Gaidinliu, and countless known and unknown heroes laid the foundation of independent India, and the responsibility of safeguarding the nation’s sovereignty, unity, and integrity today rests on the Defence Forces. “Even in adverse circumstances, the steadfast resolve of our soldiers ensures that the citizens realise their dreams in a safe environment. Their courage, commitment and discipline serve as a source of inspiration to every Indian. The nation will remain forever indebted to their unparalleled service, sacrifice, and dedication,” he said, expressing gratitude to every soldier. Defence Minister stressed that the Independence Day this year holds special significance as 2026 marks the 150th anniversary of the National Song ‘Vande Mataram’. “It is our collective responsibility to celebrate the occasion with great enthusiasm. It is not merely an anniversary, but a celebration of our collective consciousness. I am confident that this Independence Day will continue to fuel the spirit of patriotism and service to the nation within every citizen. Let us pledge to become active participants in nation-building and, by discharging our duties with dedication, make meaningful contributions towards building Viksit Bharat,” he said while concluding his address.

stories.headline: India’s wholesale inflation reaches 9.78% in July
stories.title: India’s wholesale inflation reaches 9.78% in July
stories.summary: New Delhi, Aug 14 : India’s Wholesale Price Index (WPI) inflation, with base year 2022-23, stood at 9.78 per cent year-on-year in July compared to 9.87 per cent in June, according to provisional data released by the government on Friday. The index for all commodities for July stood at 110.0, whereas it was 110.2 in June, said the Ministry of Commerce and Industry. The official statement said that inflation rates for Primary Articles, Fuel and Power, and Manufactured Products were 8.52 per cent, 20.05 per cent, and 8.29 per cent, respectively in July — compared to 7.0 per cent, 27.41 per cent, and 7.48 per cent, respectively, in June. On the other hand, the indices for Primary Articles, Fuel and Power, and Manufactured Products are 117.2, 105.4, and 108.4, respectively, in July 2026, whereas they were 116.1, 111.1, and 107.8, respectively, in June 2026. According to the data, ‘Mineral Oils (containing Petroleum Products)’, ‘Food Articles’, ‘Manufacture of Basic Metals’, ‘Non-Food Articles’, ‘Manufacture of Food Products’, and ‘Manufacture of Chemicals and Chemical Products’ have been major drivers of WPI inflation in July. The WPI Food Index observed a YoY inflation of 6.65 per cent in July 2026, compared to 6.14 per cent in June 2026. The statement further stated that the final index for the month of May 2026 has been revised from 109.9 (Provisional estimate) to 110.1. Accordingly, WPI inflation has been revised from 9.68 per cent, as per provisional estimate to 9.88 per cent as per the final estimate. Meanwhile, the final estimate of WPI for the month of May has been compiled with a weighted response rate of 98.14 per cent. Moreover, the final index of Output PPI for the month of May 2026 has been revised from 109.6 (provisional estimate) to 109.9. Also, All India Trial Input Producer Price Index (PPI) for Manufacturing Sector for July 2026 stood at 105.9 (provisional estimate). Trial Input PPI for Manufacturing Sector for the month of May has been revised from 104.9 (provisional estimate) to 106.5 (final index). —IANS

stories.headline: SC quashes FIRs against Samay Raina, four others over PwD remarks
stories.title: SC quashes FIRs against Samay Raina, four others over PwD remarks
stories.summary: New Delhi, Aug 14 : The Supreme Court on Friday quashed the FIRs registered against YouTuber and comedian Samay Raina and four other comedians in connection with offensive remarks made about Persons with Disabilities during an episode of the show 'India's Got Latent'. A Bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohan passed the order, noting that the comedians had complied with the court's earlier directions by undertaking awareness initiatives and fundraising activities for Persons with Disabilities. Apart from Raina, the relief was granted to comedians Vipul Goyal, Balraj Paramjeet Singh Ghai, Sonali Thakkar alias Sonali Aditya Desai, and Nishant Jagdish Tanwar. article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Friday (August 14, 2026) refused to interfere with the Andhra Pradesh High Court order quashing a case against Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu and Minister P. Narayana in connection with alleged irregularities in the land pooling scheme in capital Amaravati.

A Bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana said it is not inclined to interfere with the High Court order and clarified that the outcome of the petition will not have bearing on other cases, which should be adjudicated on its own merits.

Senior advocate Ranjit Kumar, appearing for Alla Rama Krishna Reddy, submitted that there were large-scale irregularities in the case which involved land of around 30,000 acres of over 25,000 farmers.
The Bench told Mr. Kumar, "On the larger issue of farmers, we are with you.
Whatever they are entitled to, we will protect." The CJI, however, pointed out that the present criminal proceedings were at the instance of a political rival and no farmer had come forward.
"Political battles should not be fought in court," the CJI told Kumar and disposed of the petition filed by Mr. Reddy challenging the July 15 order of the High Court at Amaravati.

The FIR was registered under the Prevention of Corruption Act on March 12, 2021, following a complaint by then MLA Alla Rama Krishna Reddy over the land pooling scheme announced as per a 2016 government order.
The CID, which probed the case, had named Mr. Naidu, Mr. Narayana and others as accused, and charged them under various sections of IPC, SC/ST Act, and Assigned Lands Act.
The High Court earlier stayed all further proceedings in the case following the filing of petitions by Mr. Naidu and Mr. Narayana for quashing of the case.

Under the land pooling scheme, the Andhra Pradesh government acquired agricultural land from farmers for the development of Amaravati, the capital city, in return for developed residential and commercial plots.
Under the scheme, farmers were to receive 1,000 square yards of residential land and 250 square yards of commercial land for every acre of agricultural land surrendered for the capital project.
According to the records, 28,181 landowners across 25 villages had contributed 35,215 acres of private agricultural land for the development of Amaravati.

article_sentences: A division bench of Gujarat High Court has ruled that no GST is to be levied on corporate guarantee furnished prior to October 26, 2023.
However, it has held the constitutional validity of provisions related with valuation of levying GST on corporate guarantee.
In simple terms, GST Department can impose levy on corporate guarantee furnished after October 26, 2023.

“The levy of GST on the corporate guarantee furnished prior 26th October, 2023 under Rule 28(2) is declared violative of Article 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution of India, however, levy gets attracted from this date in case the guarantees continue,” a division bench of Justices.
A S Supehia and Vaibhavi D Nanavati said in a ruling while disposing petitions by Torrent Power and 12 others.

It emphasised that he retroactive effect impinges the fundamental rights under the constitution, since the levy is unduly harsh and unfair, as taxpayers arrange their financial affairs based on the prevailing law.

It imposes an unexpected financial burden without any fault on the assessee, disrupts settled legal and financial implication, more particularly when the corporate guarantee, may stretch for long period of time.

Thus, “the imposition of levy of GST on 1 per cent valuation per annum to the corporate guarantee prior to the introduction of Rule 28(2) of the CGST Rules w.e.f October 26, 2023 is harsh and unfair to the tax payers,” it said.

The collection of tax for the period prior to introduction of Rule 28(2) will also be hit by the doctrine of unjust enrichment, since the revenue had no legal basis or authority to levy GST on corporate guarantee, which were executed prior to the date of introduction.

stories.headline: India in U.S. crosshairs again — White House report cites countries ‘enabling’ China’s tariff evasions
stories.title: India in U.S. crosshairs again — White House report cites countries ‘enabling’ China’s tariff evasions
stories.summary: The report has identified more than 40 countries associated with “elevated illegal transshipment risk”; the U.S. has named the Pune-Gujarat-Chennai belt as one of the areas enabling China
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: India is once again in the U.S.’ crosshairs, this time for allegedly allowing China to evade U.S. tariffs by routing its exports through the country.
The latest allegations are part of a new White House report called ‘The Great Transhipment Scam’.
In particular, the U.S. has named the Pune-Gujarat-Chennai belt as one of the areas “enabling” China to evade tariffs to the detriment of supply chains in the U.S.

This comes at a time when the U.S. has already imposed a 10% tariff on India for not doing enough to stop the import of goods made using forced labour, and is in the process of enacting legislation that would see tariffs of up to 100% imposed on India for its import of Russian oil.
An ongoing investigation by the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) related to excess capacity could see further tariffs on top of all this.
The U.S. had in 2018 levied tariffs ranging from 7.5% to 100% on goods from China under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 for unfair trade and tech practices.
On July 24, 2026, it added a further 12.5% tariff for forced-labour compliance gaps.
“After their imposition, Chinese exporters increasingly routed goods through third countries,” the White House report noted.

“Products that previously moved directly from China to the United States were shipped through jurisdictions where limited assembly, finishing, repackaging, relabeling, or documentation changes could create the appearance of a different national origin.”
The report has identified more than 40 countries associated with “elevated illegal transshipment risk”, with India among the top “enablers” of China’s evasion of tariffs.
“The countries that comprise China’s Shadow Transshipment Network include many of America’s largest trading partners,” the report said.
“China’s biggest enablers range from Mexico and Canada on U.S. land borders to the European Union, India, Japan, and South Korea.”
